newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Israel reassures EU on Oslo peace accords.
newsitem.headline: Israel reassures EU on Oslo peace accords.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Bejmanin Netanyahu reassured the European Union on Wednesday that his government was committed to the Oslo Middle East peace accords including an Israeli withdrawal from Hebron.

"I specifically stated that we are committed to international agreements and we expect this to be adhered to by both parties (Israel and the Palestinains)," he told a news conference after talks with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton.

"We are prepared to engage in the redoployment of Hebron and we seek a decision in principle by the Palestinian side to do so," he told a news conference in Dublin, which holds the rotating EU presidency.
Netanyahu's four-hour visit appeared to have smoothed over differences between his government and the European Union, which is seeking a bigger role in the Middle East peace process.
Netanyahu had arrived in Ireland from Spain where he had been to mark the anniversary of the historic Middle East peace conference held there in 1991.
Netanyahu said his talks with Bruton took place in a "friendly and open atmosphere" and said he saw a role for the 15-nation bloc in shaping a lasting peace.
"For too long Israel has neglected the importance of Europe and the positive contribution it can make. That is not my policy," said Netanyahu, the first Israeli leader to visit Dublin.
Bruton said his talks with Netanyahu were "exceptionally friendly and useful" and followed a visit in October by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
"We were able to see in the two presentations a will to move forward with the peace process and potential areas of agreeement between the parties," he said.
Arafat lobbied the EU to put pressure on Israel to carry out the 1993 Oslo peace accords and said he backed EU attempts to play a bigger role in fashioning a Middle East peace.

The EU has issued statements critical of Israel's handling of Palestinian unrest in recent months and has been at odds with Netanyahu's government over its intention to hold talks with Palestinian leaders in the disputed city of Jerusalem.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring incurred Israeli wrath by insisting that an EU fact-finding troika of ministers would hold talks with the Palestinians in their political offices in Orient House, in East Jerusalem.
The Israeli government hinted that it would not meet the troika if it went to Orient House but the visit did not go ahead, averting a diplomatic standoff.
Bruton said the EU and Israeli government were in contact to try to resolve the dispute but gave no hint that a resolution was in sight.
"We are aware of the differences. That is a matter we have to discuss with a view to finding a way with which the difficulties can be resolved," Bruton told the news conference.
The EU has also criticised the failure of Israel to withdraw its troops from the West Bank city of Hebron because of concerns about the security of Israeli settlers there.
Netanyahu has said that an agreement with Palestinians on a partial Israeli troop withdrawal from Hebron is nearly complete and has accused the Palestinians of stalling a final accord.
